about: Short notes on positional ideas, in the report's own words, each pointing to where a public-domain book explains the idea. The books are on Project Gutenberg; only chapter and section titles are cited.

king_safety.label: king safety
king_safety.text: Your king is safest behind pawns that haven't moved: each pawn you push in front of it stops guarding squares the enemy pieces can then use for a direct attack, and the pushed pawn itself becomes a target. Castle early, and move those pawns only for a concrete reason, not to stop a pin that isn't there yet.

development.label: development
development.text: Get your knights and bishops into play quickly, and in the opening move pieces rather than pawns: every extra pawn or queen move is a tempo your opponent spends bringing out another piece. Bring a knight out before the bishop on the same side, and combine developing with a threat when you can.

pawn_structure.label: pawn structure
pawn_structure.text: Pawns can't move back, so your pawn structure outlasts almost everything else in the game: an isolated or backward pawn, or doubled pawns that can't protect each other, stay targets long after the moves that made them. Before a pawn move, ask which squares it will stop guarding and whether another pawn can still defend it.

cites.chapter: Chapter VI, Further Openings and Middle-games

holes_outposts.label: holes and outposts
holes_outposts.text: A hole is a square in your camp that none of your pawns can guard any more; an enemy knight or bishop that settles there can't be chased away by a pawn and usually has to be exchanged. Look at which squares a pawn move gives up before you make it, and look for such squares in your opponent's camp as outposts for your own pieces.

bishop_pair.label: bishop pair
bishop_pair.text: Your two bishops together reach squares of both colours and sweep long diagonals, so they are usually worth more than two knights, and often more than a bishop and a knight, all the more as the position opens up. Give up a bishop for a knight only for a clear reason, and keep your pair when the pawns start to come off.

cites.chapter: Chapter III, General Principles of Chess Strategy

open_files.label: open files
open_files.text: Rooks need open files: the side that occupies an open file first can use it to reach the seventh or eighth rank and tie the other side's pieces to defence. When a file opens, get a rook onto it before your opponent does.

cites.section: Manoeuvres of the Pieces, Open Files and Diagonals

passed_pawns.label: passed pawns
passed_pawns.text: A passed pawn has no enemy pawn in front of it or on the files next to it, so only pieces can stop it, and it grows stronger as pieces come off the board. When your pawns face your opponent's on one side, look for the advance that creates a passed pawn, and count whose pawn queens first.

piece_activity.label: piece activity
piece_activity.text: A piece is worth what it can do: how many squares it reaches matters more than its point value. Put your pieces where they have the most scope, and look for ways to cut an enemy piece off from the fight; a bishop or knight shut out of play is almost a piece less.

cites.section: 24. Cutting Off Pieces from the Scene of Action

space.label: space
space.text: Control of the centre gives you space: your pieces can switch quickly between the wings while your opponent's stay cramped behind their own pawns. Capablanca counts the four centre squares and notes that no violent attack succeeds without control of at least two of them.
